title: Regular separability of VASS reachability languages
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, given two finite descriptions of labeled vector addition systems with states \(V_1,V_2\) over the same finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), halts and decides whether there is a regular language \(R\subseteq\Sigma^*\) such that \[L(V_1)\subseteq R\quad\text{and}\quad R\cap L(V_2)=\varnothing?\] Each \(L(V_i)\) is the finite-word reachability language defined below: a run starts with all counters zero and accepts only in a designated final state with all counters again zero. Dimensions are arbitrary finite input parameters and may differ between the two systems.

source_formulation.text: While there have been several decidability results for subclasses of the VASS languages \([16, 13, 12, 9, 8]\), the general case remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 1

why: Regular separators provide finite-state descriptions that include all behaviors of one counter system while excluding another. For exact reachability languages, this asks whether finite memory can distinguish behaviors whose counter values are unbounded along runs. The general decision theorem resolved a central separation question for Petri-net models, beyond earlier dimension and acceptance restrictions.
status_note: Resolved by Keskin and Meyer at LICS 2024 (DOI 10.1145/3661814.3662116). Theorem 3.1 of the checked 11 August 2025 expanded manuscript gives decidability for arbitrary-dimensional finite-word VASS reachability languages and constructs regular separators. The exact acceptance convention matches after finite language-preserving normalization. Checked on 15 September 2026; no independent Lean formalization was performed.

progress.text: Baumann, Meyer and Zetzsche identify general finite-word VASS reachability-language regular separation as open, while proving a separate result for Büchi VASS.
Keskin and Meyer publish the general decidability result at LICS 2024. Their theorem also gives Ackermannian-complete complexity and effective separator construction.
The expanded manuscript states the general decision and separator-construction theorem as Theorem 3.1. Its exact finite initial and final configurations include the zero-to-zero convention here.
The original open passage, the resolution theorem, and the LICS publication record were checked. This matching resolution warrants retirement of the historical question.

importance.reason: The unrestricted regular-separation question is a central finite-state abstraction problem for exact Petri-net/VASS reachability languages. Its resolution establishes the effective boundary and ties its complexity to Ackermannian reachability, rather than treating one restricted language family.
importance.basis: Individual assessment after matching the historical source question to the published LICS 2024 resolution.

sentences: A VASS reachability language records finite runs whose counters begin and end at specified exact values.
Regular separability asks for a finite automaton accepting every word of one language and no word of the other.
The historical question allowed arbitrary finite counter dimensions and zero-counter acceptance.
Keskin and Meyer resolved this general problem positively in their LICS 2024 paper, with an effective separator-construction theorem.
The card is retired because that published theorem covers its full mathematical target.

definitions: A vector addition system with states (VASS) is a tuple \(V=(d,Q,q_0,F,T)\), with dimension \(d\in\mathbb N\), finite nonempty state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\in Q\), final states \(F\subseteq Q\), and finite transition list \(T\subseteq Q\times\Sigma^*\times\mathbb Z^d\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,\mathbf c)\in Q\times\mathbb N^d\). A transition \((q,u,\mathbf z,q')\) takes it to \((q',\mathbf c+\mathbf z)\) if every resulting counter is nonnegative, and contributes the word \(u\) to the input label. Counters have no zero-test or other guard; disabled decrements are the only enabling restriction. A run is a finite transition sequence starting at \((q_0,\mathbf0)\), with all intermediate counter vectors nonnegative. Its label is the ordered concatenation of transition labels, and it accepts exactly when it ends at \((q_f,\mathbf0)\) for some \(q_f\in F\). The zero-step run is allowed. A language is regular if it is accepted by a deterministic finite automaton with a finite transition table, one start state and a set of final states. Both system descriptions explicitly list states, transitions and label words; counter updates are signed binary integers. One uniform machine must cover all dimensions and all input sizes, without a promise of disjointness. The question concerns exact total decidability, with no time, space, or separator-size bound stipulated. It concerns finite runs and exact final counter values, rather than infinite Büchi acceptance or acceptance with arbitrary final counter values.
answer_criterion: The historical target requires a complete Lean-checked proof of total decidability for exactly the input model in the formal statement, or a proof of its negation. The published resolution answers it positively: a qualifying formalization must establish termination and correctness on all pairs of finite-word reachability VASS. A separator for selected inputs, an algorithm for a fixed dimension only, or a theorem about coverability or infinite-word languages would not establish the full quantified target.

context_blocks.text: Two counter systems may describe different sets of observable finite action sequences. Separation asks for an ordinary finite automaton whose accepted language lies between them. Disjointness is necessary, but the separator must also have a finite-state representation; the decision problem quantifies over automata of every finite size.

The 2023 Büchi-VASS paper deliberately distinguishes its infinite-word result from this then-open finite-word problem. Requiring all counters to be zero at the end records exact reachability. Allowing leftover counter values changes the acceptance condition and leads to a different separation problem.

Keskin and Meyer subsequently proved decidability for the full reachability-language problem and effective construction of separators when they exist. The theorem allows arbitrary finite counter dimensions, so it covers this historical card. The card is archived as resolved rather than retained as an open benchmark.

resolution.scope_match: The theorem treats finite-word N-VASS reachability languages of arbitrary dimension with exact finite endpoint configurations. Zero initial and final vectors are included. Multiple final states can be joined to one new final state by empty-label zero updates, and finite-word transition labels can be expanded into finite chains of letter or empty-label transitions. These finite effective normalizations preserve the language.
